claims.text: When a Pulumi `Output<T>` is used as if it were a plain value (for example, string-interpolated), the resulting log line, generated file, or resource property contains placeholder text such as `Calling [toString] on an [Output<T>] is not supported` instead of the actual value.
The exact placeholder message text emitted by Pulumi when `toString` is called on an Output is `Calling [toString] on an [Output<T>] is not supported`.

The page /docs/iac/operations/troubleshooting/output-values/ ('Output value errors') exists and describes the `Calling [toString] on an [Output<T>] is not supported` symptom and other symptoms of treating an output as if it were already a plain value.

The Pulumi docs page at /docs/iac/operations/troubleshooting/output-values/ exists and covers diagnosing errors that arise from stringifying an output value, branching on an output value, or reading an output value as if it were a plain value.
In Pulumi programs, stringifying, branching on (e.g. using in a conditional), or reading an Output value as if it were a plain value causes errors.
Pulumi Cloud returns the error message "409 conflict: Another update is currently in progress" when an update is attempted while another update is already running on the stack.
The Pulumi docs page /docs/iac/operations/troubleshooting/update-conflicts/ exists.
Pulumi Cloud can return 500 internal server errors, and the page /docs/iac/operations/troubleshooting/server-errors/ covers handling them.
The Pulumi docs page /docs/iac/operations/troubleshooting/post-step-errors/ exists and covers post-step event failures and engine bugs.
The Pulumi docs page /docs/iac/operations/troubleshooting/connection-issues/ exists and covers network connectivity and proxy problems.

The Pulumi CLI produces a `read ".pulumi/meta.yaml"` error when it cannot access a self-managed (DIY) state backend, and this is documented at /docs/iac/operations/stack-management/using-a-diy-backend/ under the anchor #error-reading-pulumimetayaml.
The Pulumi docs page /docs/iac/operations/troubleshooting/destroy-failures/ exists and covers scenarios where `pulumi destroy` fails.
The Pulumi docs page /docs/iac/operations/troubleshooting/interrupted-updates/ exists and covers recovering from interrupted deployments.

On macOS Apple Silicon, running x86_64 binaries under Rosetta 2 can cause Pulumi crashes or hangs (architecture mismatch), and the page /docs/iac/operations/troubleshooting/architecture-mismatch/ covers fixing this.
The Pulumi docs page /docs/iac/operations/continuous-delivery/troubleshooting/ exists and covers continuous integration and deployment pipeline issues.
The Pulumi docs page /docs/iac/operations/stack-management/editing-state-files/ exists and describes safe techniques for modifying Pulumi state files.
A recently deleted Pulumi stack can be recovered from the Pulumi Cloud console, including after an accidental `pulumi stack rm --force`.
Pulumi CLI supports `--target` and `--exclude` options that limit operations to specific resources, which can be used when a stuck or misbehaving resource is blocking a wider update.
The Pulumi docs page /docs/iac/operations/debugging/logging/ covers automatic logging, CLI verbose logging, and program logging for debugging and diagnostics.
Pulumi provides pre-release (dev) builds that can be installed to access bug fixes that have not yet shipped in a stable release.
Pulumi Community Slack (slack.pulumi.com) offers community support.
A Pulumi guide for filing GitHub issues exists at /docs/support/filing-issues/ and explains how to report bugs in the right repository.
Running `pulumi logs share` securely sends the logs from a failed operation to the Pulumi team, and the logging guide has an #automatic-logging section covering this.
Pulumi offers paid support options via its contact page.

The Pulumi logging docs page /docs/iac/operations/debugging/logging/ has a section anchored #cli-verbose-logging covering verbose logging, which replaced the old #verbose-logging section on the troubleshooting page.

There is a new update-conflicts page at /docs/iac/operations/troubleshooting/update-conflicts/ that replaced the old #conflict section on the troubleshooting page, tracked in pulumi/pulumi issue #20846.
Pulumi resource properties are represented as Outputs rather than plain values, because their real values are not known until the resource providing them has been created or updated.
Representing resource properties as Outputs is central to how Pulumi builds a dependency graph and runs `pulumi preview`.
The docs page at /docs/iac/concepts/inputs-outputs/#outputs exists and describes Outputs.
Pulumi docs pages exist at /docs/iac/concepts/inputs-outputs/apply/ ('Accessing single outputs with Apply') and /docs/iac/concepts/inputs-outputs/all/ ('Working with multiple outputs').
If an output value is concatenated, logged, or otherwise converted to a string directly instead of via `apply` or an equivalent helper, Pulumi does not raise an error by default.
When an output is converted to a string directly, Pulumi silently substitutes a placeholder message in place of the value.
In TypeScript, interpolating an Output (e.g. `${bucket.bucketName}`) in a template literal silently produces a broken string and does not throw an exception.

In TypeScript, the string produced by converting an Output to string contains the literal text `Calling [toString] on an [Output<T>] is not supported`, followed by guidance to use `apply` or `pulumi.interpolate`.
In TypeScript, calling `JSON.stringify()` on an Output, or letting one flow into a JSON body, produces a `Calling [toJSON] on an [Output<T>] is not supported` string rather than the value.
In Python, using an Output in an f-string produces a broken string and logs a warning, and no exception is raised.
In Python, the string produced by converting an Output to string contains the literal text `Calling __str__ on an Output[T] is not supported`.
In Python, Pulumi logs a warning when an Output is converted to a string via __str__.
In Python, passing an Output to `json.dumps()` fails with `TypeError: Object of type Output is not JSON serializable`.
In Python, `Output.json_dumps()` is the Pulumi API to use for serializing an Output to JSON.
In Go, passing a `pulumi.StringOutput` where a `string` is expected is a compile error rather than a runtime error.
In Go, a value can be resolved from an Output using `ApplyT` and the result passed on.
In C#, interpolating an Output (e.g. `{bucket.BucketName}`) in a string silently produces a broken string and does not throw an exception.
In C#, the string produced by converting an Output to string contains the literal text `Calling [ToString] on an [Output<T>] is not supported`, followed by guidance to use `Apply` or `Output.Format`.

When an Output is converted to a string, the program still runs and `pulumi up` succeeds, with the placeholder text only surfacing later in a log line, generated config file, or downstream resource property.

Setting the environment variable `PULUMI_ERROR_OUTPUT_STRING=true` (supported in TypeScript, Python, and C#) makes converting an Output to a string throw an exception at the point of the mistake instead of returning the placeholder text.
The `PULUMI_ERROR_OUTPUT_STRING` environment variable is supported in TypeScript, Python, and C# but not Go.
`pulumi.interpolate` and `pulumi.concat` are string-composition helpers for Outputs in TypeScript.
`Output.concat`, `Output.format`, and `Output.json_dumps` are string-composition helpers for Outputs in Python.
`pulumi.Sprintf` and `pulumi.JSONMarshal` are string-composition/serialization helpers for Outputs in Go.
`Output.Format` is a string-composition helper for Outputs in C#.

A value read from an Output inside an `apply`/`Apply` callback is only available inside that callback (or in another output derived from it); assigning it to an outer variable and using it outside the callback does not work.

The `apply` callback runs asynchronously once the output resolves, which is generally after the rest of the program's top-level code has finished running, so reading an outer variable assigned in the callback yields `undefined`.
The `apply` callback runs when the Pulumi engine resolves the dependency graph, not on the program's clock, so adding a delay does not fix reading the value outside the callback.

Passing an Output directly as the input to a resource (e.g. `bucket: bucket.bucketName` on `aws.s3.BucketObject`) lets Pulumi resolve the dependency without needing `apply`, and is usually the better option.
Most Pulumi resource inputs accept Outputs as well as plain values.
A handful of positions, such as a resource's logical name, cannot accept an Output.
This page has a section anchored at #using-an-output-as-a-resource-name-a-map-key-or-a-loop-bound.

In a dynamically typed language, an `if` on a Pulumi Output evaluates the Output object itself rather than its eventual value, so the condition is generally always true regardless of what the output resolves to.
In a statically typed language, an `if` on an Output is usually a compile error because an `Output<bool>` is not a `bool`.
A value known when the program starts, such as a stack configuration setting read with `pulumi.Config`, an environment variable, or a hardcoded flag, is a plain value and can be branched on normally.
When a branch depends on a resource's output, the branch must move inside `apply`, expressing both outcomes as values rather than program structure.
In TypeScript, `if (vpc.vpcId)` branches on the Output object and not its value, whereas `vpc.vpcId.apply(...)` derives a new Output whose value depends on the branch.

Because branches on outputs cannot be expressed as separate blocks of resource-creation code, the program usually needs restructuring so both possible sets of resources are described unconditionally, or the branch made on a plain config value.
A resource's logical name (first constructor argument), loop bounds, and map keys used while authoring a program must be known plain values while the program is being evaluated.
Passing an Output as a resource logical name, loop bound, or map key fails to compile in TypeScript, Go, and C#, where these positions are typed as plain strings or numbers.
In Python, passing an Output as a resource's logical name raises `TypeError: Expected resource name to be a string`.
In Python, using an Output as a loop bound (`range(some_output)`) raises `TypeError: 'Output' object cannot be interpreted as an integer`.
In Python, using an Output as a dictionary key does not raise an error; Python compares and hashes the Output object itself, so the lookup silently keys on the wrong thing.

When resource names or counts depend on data only known after a resource is created, one fix is to provision the dependent resources in a later, separate stack that consumes the first stack's outputs through a `StackReference`.
The Pulumi docs page /docs/iac/concepts/stacks/ has a #stackreferences section describing StackReference.
Trying to `await` an Output or read its value synchronously either doesn't compile, fails at runtime, or quietly returns placeholder text instead of the value.
Pulumi has no supported way to block a program and pull a resolved value out of an Output synchronously.

Synchronously unwrapping an Output is unsupported because it would defeat building the dependency graph up front, since the engine would need the value before finishing determining the order to create resources.
`pulumi stack output <name>` reads a single stack output from the CLI after a deployment.
A `StackReference` from another Pulumi program consumes one stack's outputs as another stack's inputs.
The Automation API exposes an `outputs` field on the result of running an update (for example `res.Outputs` in Go).
The Pulumi docs page /docs/iac/concepts/automation-api/ exists and documents the Automation API.

`pulumi stack output`, `StackReference`, and the Automation API outputs field all read a value that has already resolved, rather than unwrapping an in-flight Output within the program that created it.
